title: Trump commutes Curtis McDonald’s life sentence
description_medium: On October 21, 2020, Trump commuted Curtis McDonald’s life sentence for a drug-trafficking and money-laundering case. McDonald had been convicted in 1996 and served nearly 24 years. The White House said he was a first-time offender with good conduct, prison work and education achievements, and mentoring service; it did not specify the commuted term in its announcement.
description_long:
Curtis McDonald was convicted in 1996 in a federal drug-trafficking and money-laundering case and sentenced to life in prison. By October 2020, he had served nearly 24 years. The White House described him as a first-time offender with a strong conduct record who had held prison jobs, completed education courses, and mentored other prisoners through the Mentors for Life program. It quoted McDonald acknowledging that he had broken the law and describing his efforts to change.

Trump signed a commutation of McDonald’s sentence on October 21, 2020, along with grants for four other prisoners. The White House said the recipients’ post-conviction conduct and efforts to help others informed its decision. Its public announcement did not state the replacement term for McDonald’s life sentence, so the precise sentence change is not established here. The clemency was a reduction of punishment, not a pardon or a reversal of the underlying conviction.
source_access_notes: White House October 21, 2020 statement read for conviction history, prison record, stated rationale, and commutation; DOJ commutations table read for original sentence and offenses.
rationale: The White House gives a recipient-specific account and rationale; DOJ records the life sentence and offenses. The White House release does not state the replacement term, which remains unspecified.

title: Trump commutes Rashella Reed’s sentence for public-benefits fraud
description_medium: Trump commuted Rashella Reed’s sentence on October 21, 2020. A former Atlanta public-school teacher, Reed was convicted of wire-fraud and money-laundering offenses in a public-benefits fraud scheme and sentenced to 14 years. The White House said she tutored incarcerated women and led children’s programs in prison; the clemency announcement did not specify a replacement term.
description_long:
Rashella Reed was a former Atlanta public-school teacher who was convicted of wire fraud and money laundering in a public-benefits fraud scheme. The Justice Department lists a 168-month prison term, three years of supervised release, and more than $8.2 million in restitution. While incarcerated, Reed used her teaching background to tutor other prisoners and facilitate programs for children visiting the prison, according to the White House.

On October 21, 2020, Trump commuted Reed’s sentence. The administration cited her work with other inmates and children as evidence of rehabilitation and said post-conviction efforts to improve the lives of others formed the basis for clemency. The announcement did not set out Reed’s new term or say whether other parts of her sentence, including restitution and supervised release, changed. A commutation reduces a sentence; it does not erase the convictions. Reed’s case was part of a five-person grant announced that day, which also included Curtis McDonald and three other prisoners.
source_access_notes: White House October 21, 2020 statement read for Reed’s prior work and prison programs; DOJ commutations table read for convictions, original sentence and restitution.
rationale: The White House supplies a person-specific account of Reed’s rehabilitation and dates the commutation; DOJ gives the original sentence and offenses. The public announcement does not identify the replacement term or effect on restitution.

title: Trump pardons pastor Otis Gordon for a 1993 drug conviction
description_medium: Trump granted Otis Gordon a full pardon on December 22, 2020, for a federal drug conviction. The White House said Gordon became a pastor at Life Changer’s International Ministries after his conviction and mentors at-risk youth. Senator Tim Scott supported the pardon, citing Gordon’s work with young men. The DOJ records an 85- or 86-month sentence for distribution of a controlled substance.
description_long:
Otis Gordon was sentenced to roughly seven years in federal prison after a 1993 conviction for selling or distributing a controlled substance. The White House described him as a pastor at Life Changer’s International Ministries who mentors at-risk young people. It also noted that Gordon led a prayer session at the U.S. Capitol in 2015 after the mass shooting at Charleston’s Emanuel AME Church. Senator Tim Scott supported clemency and described Gordon as a model citizen focused on helping young men avoid similar circumstances.

Trump granted Gordon a full pardon on December 22, 2020, during a round of grants and commutations. The White House framed the decision around Gordon’s religious leadership and community service since his conviction. The Justice Department’s clemency table records a sentence of 85 or 86 months and identifies the offense as distribution of a controlled substance. The public clemency statement does not provide additional case details about the underlying offense, so the account rests on the conviction and the administration’s description of Gordon’s later work.
source_access_notes: White House December 22, 2020 statement read for pardon date, ministry, Capitol prayer event, and supporter’s rationale; DOJ clemency table read for sentence and offense.
rationale: The White House statement names Gordon’s supporter and describes his post-conviction work; DOJ lists the pardon recipient, sentence and offense.

title: Trump pardons former WellCare executive Paul Behrens
description_medium: Trump pardoned Paul Behrens, WellCare’s former chief financial officer, during his final days in office in January 2021. A federal jury had convicted him of Medicaid health-care fraud and false statements over reports about behavioral-health spending. The DOJ listed a two-year prison sentence. The White House called the prosecution an overcriminalized regulatory dispute; DOJ and the Eleventh Circuit described inflated reports that reduced required Medicaid refunds.
description_long:
Paul Behrens was WellCare Health Plans’ chief financial officer when Florida investigated whether the company’s Medicaid plans had misreported spending on behavioral-health services. Federal prosecutors said inflated expense reports allowed WellCare subsidiaries to retain money that should have been returned to the state. A jury convicted Behrens in 2013 of two counts of health-care fraud and two counts of making false statements; he was sentenced to two years in prison and two years of supervised release. The Eleventh Circuit upheld the convictions.

Trump granted Behrens a full pardon in January 2021, alongside four other former WellCare executives. The DOJ list places him under a January 13 date heading, while contemporaneous coverage reported the grant with the final clemency announcement on January 20. The White House described the case as a state regulatory matter, said the reporting approach had expert support, and cited support from legal groups and scholars. That framing differed from the appellate opinion, which said the reports overstated spending and helped the company avoid Medicaid repayments. The pardon removed federal consequences of Behrens’s convictions; it did not overturn the jury’s verdict.
source_access_notes: DOJ press release read for jury findings and Medicaid reporting; Eleventh Circuit opinion read for the appellate court’s account; WUSF report read for the differing clemency and court descriptions; White House statement and DOJ clemency table read for grant and sentence. DOJ groups Behrens under January 13; contemporaneous reporting places the announcement on January 20.
rationale: The DOJ and appellate sources support the conviction, scheme and sentence; WUSF reports the contrasting White House rationale and the difference between DOJ’s listed date and the contemporaneous public announcement. The distinction is material because the administration characterized the case differently from the court that upheld the verdict.

title: Trump pardons Alex Adjmi for two decades-old financial convictions
description_medium: Trump granted Alex Adjmi a full pardon on January 19, 2021. DOJ records two federal cases: a money-laundering conviction and a separate conspiracy to commit insurance fraud, with prison, supervised-release, fine and restitution terms. The White House said he served five years and later supported community causes, including children with special needs and substance-recovery centers.
description_long:
Alex Adjmi’s clemency record covers two federal cases. The Justice Department lists a 1996 money-laundering conviction in Connecticut, followed by four years in prison, supervised release, community service, and a $125,000 fine. A second case in New York involved conspiracy to commit insurance fraud; the record lists concurrent supervised release, a fine, and restitution. The White House summarized the earlier conviction as a financial crime and said Adjmi served five years in prison.

Trump granted Adjmi a full pardon on January 19, 2021, during the final day of his presidency. The White House named community leaders who supported the request and described Adjmi’s later charitable work, including support for children with special needs and substance-recovery centers. The announcement did not give further detail about either case or explain how the supporters connected to the decision. The pardon followed the completion of the sentences recorded by DOJ and concerned convictions from the 1990s, rather than pending allegations.
source_access_notes: White House statement read for pardon, supporters, and charitable work; DOJ clemency table read for both federal case entries and sentence terms.
rationale: DOJ shows two separate cases and their listed sanctions; the White House gives the January 2021 pardon and its stated support. The administration’s short account of a single financial crime compresses the two-case history in the DOJ record.
